bean f. "woman, wife" cù m. "dog" bò f. "cow" taigh m. "house"
nom. sg. bean / a' bhean cù / an cù bò / a' bhò taigh / an taigh
gen. sg. mnà / na mnà coin / a' choin bà / na bà taighe / an taighe
dat. sg. mnaoi / air a' mhnaoi cù / air a' chù bò / air a' bhò taigh / air an taigh
voc. sg. a bhean! a choin! a bhò! —
dual dà mhnaoi dà chù dà bhò dà thaigh
nom. pl. mnathan / na mnathan coin / na coin bà / na bà taighean / na taighean
gen. pl. bhan / nam ban chon / nan con bhò / nam bò thaighean / nan taighean
dat. pl. mnathan / air na mnathan coin / air na coin bà / air na bà taighean / air na taighean
voc. pl. a mhnathan! a chona! — —

Other irregulars: dia "god" (gen. dè, pl. diathan); leabaidh "bed" (gen. leapa, pl. leapannan); sliabh "moor, mountain" (gen. slèibhe, pl. slèibhtean); latha "day" (gen. latha, pl. làithean; the old dative là in an là an-diugh); piuthar "sister" (gen. peathar, dat. piuthair, pl. peathraichean); bràthair "brother" (gen. bràthar, pl. bràithrean); mac "son" (gen. mic, pl. mic, gen. pl. mhac); nighean "daughter" (gen. nighinn, dat. nighinn, pl. nigheanan); gnè "kind" (invariable); clann "children" (collective, §3.9).

3.5 Genitive singular: the rules in brief

  1. Masculine, consonant-final: slenderise (§3.3 class I). Broad final vowel clusters change: ea → i (fear, fir), ia → è (iasc, èisc), ìo → ì (lìon, lìn), o → ui (cnoc, cnuic; port, puirt), eu → eòi (eun, eòin; feur, feòir).
  2. Feminine, consonant-final: slenderise and add -e (class II); polysyllables in -ach slenderise only (gealach, gealaich; cailleach, cailliche is the exception with -e). Already-slender feminines add -e: sràid, sràide; fìrinn, fìrinne; beinn, beinne.
  3. Class III nouns take -a and broaden if needed: muir, mara; sùil, sùla; fuil, fala; loch, locha; sneachd, sneachda; sruth, srutha.
  4. Vowel-final nouns do not change (class IV).
  5. Consonant stems add -ach, -ar, -n or syncopate (class V): cathair, cathrach; lasair, lasrach; caora, caorach; athair, athar; abhainn, aibhne.
  6. Verbal nouns have a genitive in -idh/-aidh for the -adh class (briseadh, brisidh; dealachadh, dealachaidh) and in -ain for -amh (seasamh, seasaimh): àm an dealachaidh "the time of parting"; ionad-feithimh "waiting-place" (from feitheamh). Kennings use these genitives constantly: seòmar-dìridh "ascent-room", muileann-nighe "washing-mill", cead-stiùiridh "steering-leave" (§10).

Lenition of an indefinite genitive. After a feminine noun an indefinite genitive is often lenited, most regularly when the two form a fixed phrase: fuil-ghuail "coal-blood", anail gheamhraidh "a winter breath", lèine-shamhraidh "a summer shirt". After a masculine noun it is not: pìos arain "a piece of bread", guth-sreinge "a string-voice", carbad-sluaigh "a crowd chariot". This is the pattern of the kennings (§10.3).

3.6 The dual

After dà "two" a noun stands in the dual: the singular, lenited, and for feminine nouns the dative singular form. It is the old dual of the tongue, whose feminine was the same as the dative, and Dia-thìris uses it throughout: dà làimh, dà chois.

masculine feminine (class II) feminine (other classes)
"two ___" dà bhalach, dà chù, dà bhàta dà làimh, dà chois, dà bhròig, dà chloich, dà chaileig dà shùil, dà mhnaoi, dà chathair
with the article an dà bhalach an dà làimh an dà shùil
gen. (masc.) ceann an dà bhalaich — —
  • dà does not lenite after the article: an dà chù, not *an dhà.
  • An adjective after a dual is plural and lenited: dà bhalach bheaga "two small boys", dà làimh fhuara "two cold hands".
  • For a feminine noun the form after dà is the dative, lenited: dà làimh, from làimh.
  • Counting the dual onward: dà ... dheug "twelve" (dà chù dheug), dà fhichead "forty" in the vigesimal count (§8.2).

3.7 The vocative

The vocative follows the particle a, which lenites. Before a vowel the particle is still written (a Aisling!, The grammar in brief §9).

masculine feminine
singular a + L + slender (= gen. sg.): a bhalaich!, a bhàird!, a fhir!, a Fhinn!, a Chiain! a + L + nom.: a bhean!, a mhàthair!, a Mhàiri!
vowel-initial names a Aonghais! (slenderised) a Aisling! (unchanged)
vowel-final nouns a dhuine!, a ghobha!, a ghille! (unchanged but lenited) a nighean!
plural strong plurals: nom. sg. + -a: a fheara!, a bhalacha!, a bhàrda!; weak plurals: nom. pl. + L: a chàirdean!, a dhaoine! a mhnathan!, a chaileagan!

Cian → a Chiain, Dubhan → a Dhubhain: Dia-thìris slenderises every masculine name in the vocative, by the class I rule (The grammar in brief §9). The vocative plural in -a (a fheara!) is the old form; Dia-thìris uses it in formal address and in tales, and the weak plural (a dhaoine!) everywhere else.

3.8 The genitive plural

Dia-thìris has two genitive plurals, and both are old:

form when examples
strong = nominative singular nouns whose plural is made by slenderising (class I), and old class II and III nouns with -an plurals nam balach, nam fear, nan con, nam ban, nam bròg, nan clach, nan làmh, nan sùl, nan Tuathach
weak = nominative plural nouns with plurals in -ichean, -tean, -annan, -achan, agent nouns, most loan-era and derived nouns nam bàtaichean, nan creachadairean, nam màthraichean, nan oidhcheannan, nan cathraichean

Indefinite genitive plurals are lenited: làn dhaoine "full of people", triùir chloinne "three children" (gen. sg. of the collective), fuaim bhròg "a sound of shoes", each bhalach "a boys' horse". In kennings, lenition of an indefinite genitive plural is the rule even after a masculine head: nimh-bhiastan "beastie-bane", cladhaire-chnàmh "bone-digger", seanchas-dhaoine "people-lore" (§10.3).

Old dative plural. The older tongue had a dative plural in -(a)ibh. Dia-thìris keeps it only in fixed expressions: air beulaibh "in front of" (lit. "on mouths"), air cùlaibh "behind" (lit. "on backs"), fo chasaibh "underfoot", and in verse: anns na beanntaibh.

3.9 Plural formation classes

Each noun's plural is given in the Dictionary, but plurals fall into classes:

class rule examples
internal (slenderising) slenderise the final consonant, with the class I vowel changes balach → balaich, cat → cait, each → eich, fear → fir, cù → coin, mac → mic, ceann → cinn, eun → eòin, bàrd → bàird, iasc → èisc, cnoc → cnuic, Dia-thìreach → Dia-thìrich, Tuathach → Tuathaich
-an after a broad final craobh → craobhan, làmh → làmhan, cas → casan, caileag → caileagan, uinneag → uinneagan, eilean → eileanan, loch → lochan, bròg → brògan
-ean after a slender final sràid → sràidean, sùil → sùilean, seachdain → seachdainean, iascair → iascairean
-tan / -tean adds t; often syncopates or changes the vowel beinn → beanntan, baile → bailtean, teine → teintean, coille → coilltean, cùil → cùiltean, buaile → buailtean, sliabh → slèibhtean
-aichean / -ichean nouns in a vowel, and many in -ar, -air with syncope bàta → bàtaichean, bliadhna → bliadhnaichean, leabhar → leabhraichean, litir → litrichean, obair → obraichean, cathair → cathraichean, màthair → màthraichean, athair → athraichean, abhainn → aibhnichean, tobar → tobraichean
-achan / -eachan vowel-final nouns, many masculine cridhe → cridheachan, talla → tallachan, co-ogha → co-oghaichean
-annan / -eannan oidhche → oidhcheannan, muir → marannan, leabaidh → leapannan, àm → amannan
-(e)an with syncope a medial unstressed vowel drops muileann → muilnean, ùbhal → ùbhlan, seòmar → seòmraichean, dorus → dorsan, tùr → tùir
irregular bean → mnathan, duine → daoine, bò → bà, piuthar → peathraichean, bràthair → bràithrean, latha → làithean, taigh → taighean, dia → diathan, sluagh → slòigh

Older plurals. Dia-thìris keeps its strong plurals and has not let -an take their place, as the Dictionary records: cnuic (not cnocan, which Dia-thìris keeps for the diminutive "hillock"), eòin, cinn, èisc, coin. A noun with two plurals keeps them apart in meaning: cnuic "hills" beside cnocan "hillocks"; lochan is both the plural of loch and a noun of its own, "a small loch" (pl. lochain).

Compounds pluralise the head: carbad-iarainn → carbadan-iarainn, eun-iarainn → eòin-iarainn, taigh-freiceadain → taighean-freiceadain, each-cuibhle → eich-chuibhle (the describer lenites after the slender plural, §4.1 rule 4).

Nouns after numerals take the plural from 3 to 10 (trì coin, còig brògan) and the singular after 11 and upwards (fichead cù, ceud bliadhna). A small old set keeps the singular after every numeral, relics of the old counted forms: bliadhna, latha, uair: trì bliadhna, còig latha, dà uair "twice; two o'clock". See §8.

3.10 Collective nouns

Collectives are singular in form, take singular articles and adjectives, and are referred to with the plural pronoun iad when the members are meant:

noun gender gen. dat. note
clann "children" f. cloinne cloinn a' chlann, leis a' chloinn, triùir chloinne
sluagh "people, host" m. sluaigh sluagh pl. slòigh "hosts, peoples": an dà shluagh
crodh "cattle" m. cruidh crodh an crodh agus an caoraich
muinntir "folk, household" f. muinntire muinntir muinntir an eilein
luchd "people of, load" m. luchda luchd only in compounds: luchd-turais, luchd-ciùil
feur "grass" m. feòir feur
iasc "fish" (as food) m. èisc iasc a' sireadh arain agus èisc
aodach "clothing" m. aodaich aodach
airgead "silver, money" m. airgid airgead trì buinn airgid
cuideachd "company" f. cuideachd cuideachd

With the personal numerals (§8.4) clann stands in the genitive: triùir chloinne, seachdnar chloinne (both in the tales).

4. Adjectives

Attributive adjectives follow their noun and agree with it in gender, number and case, by lenition and by endings. Predicative adjectives (tha an taigh mòr) are uninflected (Sentences §1.3). A small set of adjectives precedes the noun and forms a close compound with it (§4.5).

4.1 Lenition of the attributive adjective

The adjective is lenited:

  1. after a feminine singular noun in the nominative and dative: bean mhòr, a' bhean mhòr, air a' bhròig mhòir;
  2. after a masculine singular noun in the genitive and vocative: taigh a' bhalaich bhig, a bhalaich bhig!;
  3. after a masculine singular noun in the dative with the article: air a' bhalach mhòr, anns an taigh bheag (without the article it stays plain: air balach mòr);
  4. after a plural noun ending in a slender consonant (the strong plurals): balaich bheaga, fir mhòra, eich dhubha, coin bhàna; not after a broad plural: brògan mòra, taighean geala, ballachan dearga;
  5. after a dual: dà bhalach bheaga, dà làimh fhuara.

Everywhere else it is plain: balach mòr, am balach mòr, taighean mòra. The ordinary lenition exceptions apply (§1.2): bean làidir, bean rìoghail, sràid stàiteil, clach scaoilte.

Place names. In place names the qualifier is lenited after every generic, masculine or feminine: Baile ghorm, Cnoc bheag, Dùn thais, Cathair mhòr. In speech an adjective after a masculine noun follows rule 3 above (baile gorm). Dia-thìris keeps the always-lenited form as a fixed naming pattern (The grammar in brief §4; Names).

4.2 Case and number endings

Monosyllabic adjectives decline like nouns: slenderised in the masculine genitive, slenderised with -e in the feminine genitive, slenderised in the feminine dative, and with -a/-e in the plural. Polysyllabic adjectives, and those ending in a vowel, show only lenition (brèagha, àlainn, toilichte, dìleas, uaine), with a few polysyllables in -ach slenderising (§4.3).

Paradigm: mòr "big" with a masculine and a feminine noun

masculine: balach mòr feminine: bròg mhòr
nom. sg. balach mòr / am balach mòr bròg mhòr / a' bhròg mhòr
gen. sg. balaich mhòir / a' bhalaich mhòir bròige mòire / na bròige mòire
dat. sg. air balach mòr / air a' bhalach mhòr air bròig mhòir / air a' bhròig mhòir
voc. sg. a bhalaich mhòir! a bhròg mhòr!
dual dà bhalach mhòra dà bhròig mhòra
nom./dat. pl. balaich mhòra / na balaich mhòra brògan mòra / na brògan mòra
gen. pl. bhalach mòra / nam balach mòra bhròg mòra / nam bròg mòra

Case forms of common monosyllables

adj. meaning m. gen., f. dat. f. gen. plural comparative (§4.4)
mòr big mòir mòire mòra motha
beag small big bige beaga lugha
geal white gil gile geala gile
dubh black duibh duibhe dubha duibhe
dearg red deirg deirge dearga deirge
glas grey-green glais glaise glasa glaise
bàn fair, white bàin bàine bàna bàine
òg young òig òige òga òige
ùr new ùir ùire ùra ùire
fuar cold fuair fuaire fuara fuaire
àrd high àird àirde àrda àirde
trom heavy truim truime troma truime
crom bent cruim cruime croma cruime
fada long fada fada fada fhaide
glic wise glic glice glice glice
math good maith maithe matha fheàrr

So oidhche na gealaich ùire "the night of the new moon", air bruaichean na h-Aibhne mòire, airson a' mhargaidh mhòir "for the big market", fo bhallachan dearga a' chaisteil "under the red walls of the castle", eich bhrèagha ghil "(in the shape) of a beautiful white horse" (gen. sg. m., both lenited, in the tale of the water horse: ann an riochd eich bhrèagha ghil).

The older declension. The older tongue declined its adjectives fully, like nouns of the same stem class. Dia-thìris still declines the monosyllables in the genitive and dative as a matter of course, as the tales do.

4.3 Polysyllabic adjectives

Adjectives of two or more syllables take no plural ending and, mostly, no case ending: daoine toilichte, clann bhrèagha, na h-òrain àlainn. They still lenite by §4.1: bean bhrèagha, na balaich bhrèagha. Adjectives in -ach slenderise in the masculine genitive and the feminine dative and genitive: fearann creagach "rocky land", gen. fearainn chreagaich; adjectives already ending slender (fiadhaich) do not change: bean fhiadhaich, fearainn fhiadhaich.

4.4 Comparison

The comparative form is made by slenderising and adding -e (after a slender vowel -e alone), so that for regular adjectives it is identical with the feminine genitive singular:

positive comparative positive comparative
luath "fast" luaithe domhain "deep" doimhne
òg "young" òige ìseal "low" ìsle
geal "white" gile soilleir "bright" soilleire
sean "old" sine cruaidh "hard" cruaidhe
fuar "cold" fuaire fliuch "wet" fliche
blàth "warm" blàithe glic "wise" glice
àrd "high" àirde brèagha "beautiful" brèagha (vowel-final: unchanged)

Irregular comparatives

positive comparative note
math "good" fheàrr nas fheàrr, as fheàrr, na b' fheàrr; is fheàrr leam "I prefer"
dona "bad" miosa
mòr "big" motha (older mò)
beag "small" lugha
fada "long" fhaide na b' fhaide (tale of the water horse)
furasta "easy" fhasa
duilich "difficult" dorra (also duilghe)
teth "hot" teotha
goirid "short" giorra
làidir "strong" treasa (also làidire)
faisc "near" faisce
ionmhainn "dear" annsa old; in verse and in is annsa leam "I love best"
tric "frequent" trice
cumhang "narrow" cumhainge

The fh- of fheàrr, fhaide, fhasa is written in all positions. It is the mark of an old lenition: nas and as go back to a phrase meaning "a thing that is", which lenited the word after it.

Degrees and particles

present, future past, conditional
comparative ("bigger") nas motha na bu mhotha; na b' before a vowel or fh: na b' fheàrr, na b' òige
"than" na: nas motha na taigh, nas òige na esan na bu mhotha na an taigh
superlative ("biggest") relative as: an taigh as motha, an nighean as òige a bu: an taigh a bu mhotha, an rubha a b' fhaide an iar

The superlative is a relative clause of the copula ("the house that is biggest"), so it takes the copula's tenses (§7): as in the present and future, a bu + L in the past and conditional.

The equative. "As ... as" is cho + positive + ri (+ ris before the article): cho socair ri caora "as gentle as a sheep", cho domhainn ris an talamh "as deep as the earth"; with a clause, cho ... 's a: cho luath 's a b' urrainn dha "as fast as he could". Cho does not lenite: cho mòr, cho beag. Before a following clause of result, cho ... 's gun: bha e cho ciùin 's gun deach sianar dhiubh air a mhuin "it was so calm that six of them got on its back".

Nouns of degree. Beside the comparative, most common adjectives have a noun of degree, used for "how big", "its length": meud "size" (a mheud), fad "length" (fad na h-oidhche "all night"), leud "breadth", àirde "height", doimhne "depth", luaths "speed", teas "heat", fuachd "cold". Cia mheud? "how many?" is at root "what amount?".

Intensifiers. glè "very" + L (glè mhath, glè bheag, glè thoilichte: glè lenites every consonant, dentals included); ro "too" + L (ro fhadalach, ro mhòr); fìor "truly" + L (fìor mhath); gu math "quite" (gu math fuar); uabhasach "terribly" (uabhasach fuar).

Adverbs are made from adjectives with gu (gu h- before a vowel): gu math "well", gu luath "quickly", gu cùramach "carefully", gu h-àrd "up above", gu h-obann "suddenly".

4.5 Adjectives before the noun: the preposed set

A small closed set precedes the noun, forms a close compound with it (hyphenated with some nouns and in fixed terms), and lenites it. The noun keeps its own gender and case; the preposed adjective does not inflect.

adjective meaning mutation examples
seann (pred. sean) old L, dental block seann bhean, seann chù, seann taigh, seann duine, seann sagart; pl. seann daoine, na seann bhailtean
deagh good L deagh dhuine, deagh bhiadh, deagh shìde
droch bad L droch dhuine, droch shìde, droch bhliadhna
sàr excellent, supreme L sàr-bhàrd, sàr-ghaisgeach, sàr-mhath
fìor true, very L fìor charaid, fìor-uisce "spring water", fìor mhath
prìomh chief L prìomh-bhaile "capital town", prìomh-chathair "capital city"
àrd high, chief (in compounds) L àrd-rìgh "high king", àrd-bhàrd
ath next, re- L an ath bhliadhna, an ath sheachdain, an ath latha
dearbh very, self-same L an dearbh bhean "the very woman"
leth half, one of a pair L leth-uair, leth-bhreac "twin", leth-inbheach "half-grown"
corra odd, occasional L corra uair "now and then"
iomadh many none; singular noun iomadh bliadhna, iomadh duine
gach each none gach feascar, gach latha
a h-uile every none a h-uile duine, a h-uile nì

Seann before a noun and sean after the copula or tha are the same word, seann being the old form that leans on the noun after it: seann duine "an old man", tha e sean "he is old".

4.6 Adjective compounds

Two adjectives, or an adjective and a noun, may fuse, the second lenited: dubh-ghorm "dark blue", liath-ghlas "grey-green", ceann-mòr "big-headed" (noun + adjective), cas-rùiscte "barefoot". These count as one word for agreement: bean dhubh-ghorm.

5. Pronouns, possessives and prepositional pronouns

5.1 Personal pronouns

plain emphatic reflexive/intensive (+ fhèin)
1 sg. "I, me" mi mise mi fhèin
2 sg. "you" thu, tu thusa, tusa thu fhèin
3 sg. m. "he, him, it" e esan e fhèin
3 sg. f. "she, her, it" i ise i fhèin
1 pl. "we, us" sinn sinne sinn fhèin
2 pl./polite "you" sibh sibhse sibh fhèin
3 pl. "they, them" iad iadsan iad fhèin

There is no separate object form: Chunnaic mi e "I saw him", Chunnaic e mi "he saw me". Tu replaces thu after verb forms ending in -dh or -s (bidh tu, cuiridh tu, sheasadh tu, an robh thu? but bhios tu) and after the copula (is tu). Sibh is plural and the polite singular (The grammar in brief §9).

The emphatic forms carry contrast and stand alone: Is mise Eilidh "I am Eilidh"; na blais thusa dheth "don't you taste it". Esan and iadsan stand outside caol le caol, as the emphatic suffixes do (§5.2).

Other pronouns.

forms
demonstrative seo "this", sin "that", siud "that (yonder)"; after a noun with the article: an t-sràid seo, an loch sin; as pronouns: seo an t-airgead, Bha siud ann uair
interrogative cò "who", dè "what", cia mheud "how many", cò aca "which (of them)", ciamar "how", càite "where", carson "why", cuin(e) "when"
indefinite cuideigin "someone", rudeigin "something", duine sam bith "anyone", nì sam bith "anything", càch "the others", a chèile "each other"
pronominal nouns fear "one (m.)", tè "one (f.)": tè dhiubh "one of them (f.)", fear às dèidh fir "one after another"

A chèile takes possessive mutations after prepositions: ri chèile, le chèile, bho chèile, eadar a chèile. Cuideigin, rudeigin also stand outside caol le caol.

5.2 Emphatic suffixes

Emphasis on a pronoun that is fused into another word (a prepositional pronoun, a possessed noun, a synthetic verb form) is carried by a suffix:

person suffix after a prepositional pronoun after a possessed noun after a verb
1 sg. -sa / -se agamsa, leamsa, dhòmhsa mo thaigh-sa sheasainn-sa
2 sg. -sa / -se agadsa, ortsa, dhutsa do chù-sa —
3 sg. m. -san aigesan, airsan, dhàsan a bhàta-san —
3 sg. f. -se aicese, oirrese, dhìse a bàta-se —
1 pl. -e, -ne againne, oirnne, dhuinne ar taigh-ne sheasamaid-ne
2 pl. -se agaibhse, oirbhse, dhuibhse ur taigh-se —
3 pl. -san acasan, orrasan, dhaibhsan an taigh-san —

The suffix is written solid after a prepositional pronoun and hyphenated after a noun. Like esan, the suffixes stand outside the caol le caol law; in the older tongue they were words of their own, and they keep the freedom of separate words still. Where a solid form would clash, the hyphen is written (leis-san, ris-san, às-san, dheth-san); the traditional solid forms aigesan, airsan, leathase, bhuaithesan, uimesan, thuigesan, dhaibhsan are correct Dia-thìris, and stand outside the law as esan and iadsan do. The texts use them freely: is ann dhutsa a bha am bradan an dàn, agus chan ann dhòmhsa "it was for you the salmon was destined, not for me".

5.3 Possessives

before a consonant before a vowel before f + vowel example
mo "my" mo + L m' m' fh- mo mhàthair, m' athair, m' fhàrdach
do "your (sg.)" do + L d' d' fh- do phiuthar, d' athair, d' fhàrdach
a "his, its (m.)" a + L a a fh- a mhàthair, a athair, a fhàrdach
a "her, its (f.)" a a h- a f- a màthair, a h-athair, a fàrdach
ar "our" ar ar n- ar f- ar màthair, ar n-athair
ur "your (pl.)" ur ur n- ur f- ur màthair, ur n-athair
an "their" an, am (before b, f, m, p) an am f- am màthair, an athair, am fàrdach

The three a's ("his", "her", and the vocative particle) are told apart by their mutations alone: a chù "his dog", a cù "her dog", a choin! "O dog!".

Traces of eclipsis. ar n-, ur n- and am/an "their" are the old eclipsing possessives; of their mutation only the n- before vowels and the nasal assimilation of an → am are written in Dia-thìris (§1.6).

Possessive or aig? Inalienable things (body, kin, mind, name) take the possessive: mo cheann, mo mhàthair, m' ainm. Alienable possessions usually take the article + aig: an taigh agam "my house", na craicnean aca "their skins" (Sentences §5.1).

Possessives with verbal nouns. A pronoun object of a verbal noun is a possessive before it, fused with aig in the progressive: gam fhaicinn "seeing me", gad fhaicinn, ga fhaicinn "seeing him", ga faicinn "seeing her", ga h-ithe "eating it (f.)", gar faicinn, gur faicinn, gan faicinn, gam bualadh "hitting them"; after other particles the possessive is written in full: a dhèanamh "to do it", airson a shlìobadh "in order to stroke it", mo chuideachadh "to help me". See Sentences §2.5–2.6.

5.4 Prepositions: case and mutation

ann an / ann am in dat. none anns an, anns a'; san, sa ann an

Compound prepositions (air beulaibh, ri taobh, an aghaidh, mu dheidhinn, airson, an dèidh, os cionn, air feadh, a dh'aindeoin) take the genitive of a noun and a possessive for a pronoun: os cionn a' chaolais "above the strait", os mo chionn "above me", mu mo dheidhinn "about me", nam measc "among them". Their uses belong to Sentences §8.4.

5.5 Prepositional pronouns

A simple preposition fuses with a following personal pronoun. The tables give the plain form, then the emphatic (§5.2).

aig "at", air "on", do "to", le "with"

Aisde "out of her" is written with d, the older spelling, which Dia-thìris has kept. Ann "in it (m.)" is also the adverb "there, in existence": Bha siud ann uair "there was once (that)".

1 sg. rium / riumsa fodham / fodhamsa umam / umamsa thugam / thugamsa

ro tro thar eadar
1 sg. romham tromham tharam —
2 sg. romhad tromhad tharad —

3 sg. f. roimhpe troimhpe thairte —

Emphatics add the same suffixes (romhamsa, thartasan). Thairis is also the adverb "across, over": a dhol thairis air an drochaid "to cross the bridge". Roimhe is also "before (in time)": air an t-each fhaicinn roimhe "had seen the horse before". Gun "without" has no fused forms; it takes às aonais + possessive: às m' aonais "without me".

Fixed idioms built on these (full treatment in Sentences §5): possession tha cù agam; states tha an t-acras orm; liking is toil leam; ability is urrainn dhomh; ownership is leamsa e; necessity tha agam ri falbh; "there" tha e ann; naming ris an canadh daoine Loch Dubh "which people used to call Loch Dubh".

5.6 Preposition + possessive

The possessives fuse with some prepositions. Dia-thìris writes these contractions as single words without an apostrophe, and the tales use them so: na mhuing "in its mane", nam bheul "in my mouth", na fhuil "in his blood", leum iad dhan uisce nan ròin "they leapt into the water as seals (lit. in their seals)".

possessive ann an + poss. aig + poss. (with verbal noun) do + poss. mutation
my nam gam dhom L
your (sg.) nad gad dhod L
his na ga dha L
her na ga dha h- before vowel
our nar gar dhar n- before vowel
your (pl.) nur gur dhur n- before vowel
their nan, nam gan, gam dhan, dham none

Ann an + possessive is also the predicative "as": bha i na bean-phòsta chòir "she was a kind wife (lit. in her kind wife)", tha e na iascair "he is a fisherman". See Sentences §1.3 and §2.7.

With the other prepositions Dia-thìris writes the possessive in full, as the tales do (fo a chòta "under his coat", le a òrdag "with his thumb", bho mo sheanmhair "from my grandmother", gu a màthair "to her mother"); in speech these run together as fom, lem, bhom, gum, and that pronunciation may be written in dialogue:

bho fo le mu ri gu de tro ro
my bhom fom lem mum rim gum dhem trom rom
your (sg.) bhod fod led mud rid gud dhed trod rod
his, her bho a fo a le a mu a ri a gu a de a tro a ro a

6. Verbs

6.1 The shape of the verb

A Dia-thìris verb is cited by its root, which is the second person singular imperative (tog! "lift!", bris! "break!"), and its verbal noun (togail, briseadh), which is lexical. The Dictionary gives both.

The finite verb has three simple tenses (past, future, conditional), an imperative, a relative future, and an impersonal (passive) form of each. There is no simple present: the present and all aspectual tenses are periphrastic, built on bi + a particle + the verbal noun (tha mi a' togail "I am lifting", tha mi air togail "I have lifted"); those belong to Sentences §2.

Every tense has an independent form, used when the verb begins its clause or follows ma or the relative a, and a dependent form, used after the particles cha, an, nach, gun, mura and the like. It is the old distinction of absolute and conjunct forms, which Dia-thìris keeps in the future (togaidh / tog) and in the irregular verbs (chunnaic / faca), and marks in the past with the particle do.

Person is marked by a following pronoun (analytic forms: thog mi, thog thu), except in a set of synthetic forms where the ending carries the person: the first person singular and plural of the conditional (thogainn, thogamaid) and of the imperative (togam, togamaid). The older tongue had synthetic forms throughout, and these few are what is left of them. Dia-thìris uses the synthetic forms as the norm and does not add a pronoun to them: thogainn "I would lift", not *thogainn mi.

6.2 The regular verb: full paradigms

Four models: tog "lift, build" (broad), bris "break" (slender), òl "drink" (vowel-initial) and fàg "leave" (f-initial). The ending is broad or slender by the last vowel of the root; the initial is lenited in the independent past and conditional, with dh' before a vowel and before fh + vowel (dh'fhàg); before fh + consonant the lenited form stands alone (fhreagair "answered", fhliuch "wetted", as in the tale of Fionn).

Past

tog bris òl fàg
independent thog mi, thog thu, thog e, thog i, thog sinn, thog sibh, thog iad bhris mi … dh'òl mi … dh'fhàg mi …
dependent (after cha, an, nach, gun, mura) do thog: cha do thog, an do thog? do bhris do dh'òl do dh'fhàg
impersonal thogadh "was lifted"; dep. do thogadh bhriseadh; do bhriseadh dh'òladh; do dh'òladh dh'fhàgadh; do dh'fhàgadh

Future (also the habitual present: òlaidh mi uisce gach latha "I drink water every day")

tog bris òl fàg
independent togaidh mi, togaidh tu, togaidh e … brisidh mi … òlaidh mi … fàgaidh mi …
dependent tog: cha tog, an tog?, nach tog, gun tog bris: cha bhris, am bris? òl: chan òl, an òl? fàg: chan fhàg, am fàg?
relative a thogas a bhriseas a dh'òlas a dh'fhàgas
impersonal togar (indep. and dep.): cha togar brisear òlar fàgar

Conditional

tog bris òl fàg
1 sg. thogainn bhrisinn dh'òlainn dh'fhàgainn
2 sg. thogadh tu bhriseadh tu dh'òladh tu dh'fhàgadh tu
3 sg. thogadh e, i bhriseadh e, i dh'òladh e, i dh'fhàgadh e, i
1 pl. thogamaid bhriseamaid dh'òlamaid dh'fhàgamaid
2 pl. thogadh sibh bhriseadh sibh dh'òladh sibh dh'fhàgadh sibh
3 pl. thogadh iad bhriseadh iad dh'òladh iad dh'fhàgadh iad
impersonal thogtadh bhristeadh dh'òltadh dh'fhàgtadh
dependent togainn, togadh, togamaid, togtadh brisinn, briseadh, briseamaid, bristeadh òlainn, òladh, òlamaid, òltadh fàgainn, fàgadh, fàgamaid, fàgtadh

The conditional is also the habitual past, the tense of the tales: sheasadh i aig an doras "she would stand at the door", thigeadh e às an loch "it would come out of the loch".

Imperative

tog bris òl fàg
1 sg. "let me …" togam briseam òlam fàgam
2 sg. tog bris òl fàg

2 pl./polite togaibh brisibh òlaibh fàgaibh

Summary of endings

form broad slender mutation
past — — L (dh' before vowel, fh); dep. do + L
future -aidh -idh none; dep. = root
future relative -as -eas L (dh')
future impersonal -ar -ear none
conditional 1 sg. -ainn -inn L (dh'); dep. none
conditional 1 pl. -amaid -eamaid L (dh'); dep. none
conditional other persons -adh -eadh L (dh'); dep. none
conditional impersonal -tadh -teadh L (dh'); dep. none
past impersonal -adh -eadh L (dh'); dep. do + L
imperative 1 sg. -am -eam none
imperative 3 sg./pl. -adh -eadh none
imperative 1 pl. -amaid -eamaid none
imperative 2 pl. -aibh -ibh none
imperative impersonal -tar -tear none

The past impersonal and the conditional third person are spelled alike (bhriseadh "was broken" and "would break"); context and the dependent forms (do bhriseadh against briseadh) tell them apart. The relative takes dh' like the past before a vowel or fh + vowel: a dh'òlas, ma dh'èisteas tu (tale of the Old Ones), nuair a dh'fhaighnicheas (tale of the Tuathaich).

6.3 Stem types

Verbs in -ich are slender throughout: ceannaich "buy": cheannaich, ceannaichidh, cheannaicheadh, cheannaichinn, cheannaicheamaid, a cheannaicheas, ceannaichear, cheannaichteadh. Their verbal noun is usually -achadh (§6.6), and their participle -ichte.

Syncopating verbs. Roots of two syllables whose second vowel is short and unstressed lose it before a vowel-initial ending, and the consonant cluster then takes the class of the first vowel:

root meaning future conditional 2 pl. imperative verbal noun
caidil sleep cadlaidh chadladh, chadlainn cadlaibh cadal
foscail open fosclaidh dh'fhoscladh fosclaibh foscladh
innis tell innsidh dh'innseadh innsibh innse
bruidhinn speak bruidhnidh bhruidhneadh bruidhnibh bruidhinn
freagair answer freagraidh fhreagradh freagraibh freagairt
tachair happen tachraidh thachradh — tachairt
labhair speak (formal) labhraidh labhradh labhraibh labhairt
iomair row iomraidh dh'iomradh iomraibh iomradh

These eight and a dozen more (ceangail, fuascail, seachain, coisinn, siubhail, tadhail…) syncopate before every vowel-initial ending, and keep the full root in the past, the 2 sg. imperative and the consonant-initial impersonals (chaidil, caidil, chaidilteadh).

Verbs in a long vowel or -gh add endings without change: suidh "sit": shuidh, suidhidh; nigh "wash": nighidh, nigheadh; dìrich "climb" is an -ich verb.

6.4 The impersonal (autonomous) forms

Every tense has an impersonal form, "one lifts / it is lifted", with no subject; the agent, if named, follows le. They are the old passive of the tongue, and Dia-thìris uses them in every register: Chan fhacas iad a-riamh tuilleadh "they were never seen again"; cha d' fhuaireadh sceul orra "no trace of them was found"; rugadh mi ann an Seann Dunn "I was born in Seann Dunn"; gum faicte ròn mòr glas "that a big grey seal would be seen".

tense ending tog bris
past -adh / -eadh + L thogadh (dep. do thogadh) bhriseadh (dep. do bhriseadh)
future -ar / -ear togar brisear
conditional -tadh / -teadh + L thogtadh (dep. togtadh) bhristeadh (dep. bristeadh)
imperative -tar / -tear togtar bristear

The pronoun object of an impersonal stays a pronoun: thogadh e "it was lifted", bhriseadh iad "they were broken". The periphrastic passive with rach (chaidh a dhèanamh "it was made") and with bi + air (tha e air a dhèanamh "it has been made") are in Sentences §4.

6.5 The relative future

After the relative particle a ("who, which, that"), after ma "if", and after the conjunctions built on the relative (nuair a "when", mar a "as", cho fad 's a "as long as"), the future is the relative future in -as/-eas, lenited: an duine a sheasas "the man who will stand", ma thogas tu "if you lift", nuair a dh'fhaighnicheas clann nan Tuathach "when the children of the Tuathaich ask", cho fad 's a bhios gual fon talamh "as long as there is coal under the ground". The irregular verbs use their independent future (§6.9): a nì, a chì, a thèid. The older tongue had relative forms in -as in the present; they have lived on in the future, and Dia-thìris uses them wherever a relative future is possible; the plain future after a (*an duine a seasaidh) is not Dia-thìris.

6.6 Verbal noun formation

The verbal noun names the action and does the work of the non-finite verb (Sentences §2). It is lexical, but most verbs fall into these classes:

class formation examples
-adh / -eadh root + -adh/-eadh; the largest class, and the default for new verbs bris → briseadh, pòs → pòsadh, glan → glanadh, bual → bualadh, scrìobh → scrìobhadh, loisc → loscadh, dùisc → dùscadh, dùin → dùnadh, las → lasadh
-amh / -eamh root + -amh/-eamh seas → seasamh, dèan → dèanamh, caith → caitheamh, feith → feitheamh
-ail / -eil root + -ail/-eil fàg → fàgail, tog → togail, gabh → gabhail, cùm → cumail, leig → leigeil, tilg → tilgeil
-tainn / -tinn root + -tainn/-tinn cluinn → cluinntinn, lean → leantainn, fan → fantainn, seall → sealltainn, can → cantainn, tuit → tuiteam (-eam, an old variant)
-sinn root + -sinn tuig → tuigsinn, creid → creidsinn, ruig → ruigsinn, trèig → trèigsinn
-inn / -ainn root + -inn/-ainn faic → faicinn, faigh → faighinn, feuch → feuchainn, tig → tighinn
-achadh / -eachadh -ich verbs: -ich → -achadh/-eachadh cruinnich → cruinneachadh, smaoinich → smaoineachadh, ionnsaich → ionnsachadh, tòisich → tòiseachadh, coinnich → coinneachadh, sàraich → sàrachadh, bàsaich → bàsachadh, soilleirich → soilleireachadh
-ach, -eachd, -igh -ich verbs, older short forms ceannaich → ceannach, fuirich → fuireach, falaich → falach, coisich → coiseachd, èirich → èirigh, dìrich → dìreadh
-achd / -eachd èist → èisteachd, marcaich → marcachd
-e root + -e ith → ithe, nigh → nighe, suidh → suidhe, guidh → guidhe, innis → innse
-aidh / -airt / -al / -ad smaller classes iarr → iarraidh, freagair → freagairt, tachair → tachairt, labhair → labhairt, caidil → cadal, ceangail → ceangal, gluais → gluasad
zero verbal noun = root òl, ruith, fàs, snàmh, seinn, leum, dìon, gairm, cluich, falbh, ràn
irregular rach → dol, thig → tighinn, abair → ràdh, thoir → toirt, beir → breith, bi → bhith, dèan → dèanamh, faic → faicinn, faigh → faighinn

Older verbal nouns. Where a verbal noun might have been levelled to a commoner pattern, Dia-thìris keeps the older one: fantainn "staying" (from fan), cantainn "saying" (from can), labhairt "speaking" (from labhair), sealltainn "looking", trèigsinn "forsaking". Fuireach (from fuirich) is the usual word for "living, dwelling"; fantainn is "waiting, remaining".

The genitive of the verbal noun is used after another noun and as the object of a verbal noun: -adh → -aidh/-idh (àm a' bhrisidh; seòmar-dìridh "ascent-room", from dìreadh), -achadh → -achaidh (àm a' chruinneachaidh), -amh → -aimh (ionad-feithimh), -ail unchanged (obair-togail "building work"). See §3.5.

6.7 Participles

The past participle ("broken, lifted") is the root + -te (-ta after some broad roots), with -ichte for -ich verbs. It is an adjective: it lenites after a feminine noun and does not take a plural ending.

root participle root participle
bris briste "broken" pòs pòsta "married"
dùin dùinte "shut" dèan dèanta "done, made"
caill caillte "lost" reòth reòta "frozen"
loisc loiscte "burnt" toll tollta "holed"
scrìobh scrìobhte "written" abair ràite "said"
foscail foscailte "open" croch crochte "hanged"
ceannaich ceannaichte "bought" sàraich sàraichte "oppressed"
tog togte "built" cruinnich cruinnichte "gathered"

An cnoc loiscte "the burnt hill" (tale of the coal-blood), bean phòsta "a married woman", bròg thollta "a holed shoe" (the kenning for "flat tyre"). The ending is written -te after a broad consonant too (togte, pòsta beside loiscte); the ending stands outside caol le caol.

Two other adjectival forms of the verb:

  • Gerundive with ri + verbal noun: ri fhaicinn "to be seen", ri reic "for sale", ri dèanamh "to be done".
  • Potential with so- "easy to" and do- "hard/impossible to" (§9.5): so-dhèanta "feasible", do-dhèanta "impossible", so-thuigsinn "easy to understand".

6.8 Preverbal particles and their mutations

The particles are syntax (Sentences §3.3–3.4); their effect on the verb's form is morphology:

particle meaning takes mutation examples
cha, chan not dependent L, but not d, t; chan before a vowel and lenited f cha bhris, cha sheas, cha dèan, cha tèid, chan òl, chan fhaic, cha do thog, cha tuirt
an, am question dependent none (am before b, f, m, p) an tog?, am bris?, am faic?, an do thog?
nach negative question; "that … not" dependent none nach tog?, nach eil?
gun, gum that dependent none gun tog, gum bris, gun do thog
mura, mur if not dependent none mura tog, mura do thog
ma if independent (relative future) L ma thogas tu, ma dh'èisteas tu, ma chaidh
nan, nam if (unreal) conditional, dependent none nan togadh tu, nam biodh
a who, which independent (relative future) L a thogas, a bhios, a thàinig
na don't imperative h- before vowel na tog, na h-òl
mus, gus before, until dependent none (gus an + dependent) mus tig an stoirm, gus an do shoilleirich an latha

6.9 The irregular verbs

Eleven verbs are irregular: bi and ten others. Most of them build their tenses on more than one stem, old roots of different shape brought together under one meaning (faic: past chunnaic, future chì). The tables below give every form: past, future, conditional (1 sg., 1 pl. and other persons), relative, the imperative of every person, and the impersonals. In each table, indep. is the independent form and dep. the dependent.

bi "be"

indep. dep. after cha impersonal (indep. / dep.)
present tha bheil (a bheil?, gu bheil) chan eil; nach eil thathar / eilear
past bha robh (an robh?, gun robh) cha robh bhathar / robhar

verbal noun bhith (a bhith)

The present relative is the independent tha (an duine a tha an-seo), shortened to a th' before a vowel (dè an t-ainm a th' ort?). Thathar ag ràdh "it is said" is the impersonal present.

abair "say"

indep. dep. impersonal (indep. / dep.)

The defective arsa, ars "said" introduces or follows direct speech: ars an guth "said the voice", ars esan. Abair is also the exclamation "what a …!": Abair naidheachd!

Rugadh mi "I was born"; rug i triùir chloinne dha "she bore him three children"; beir air "catch hold of it". Beir and thoir share the conditional bheireadh.

indep. dep. impersonal (indep. / dep.)

Gum faicte ròn mòr glas (tale of the seal wife) uses the short dependent impersonal faicte; both it and faicteadh are Dia-thìris. Seall "look" is the usual imperative in speech (seall air a mhuing "look at its mane").

6.10 Defective and modal verbs

verb meaning forms example
feum must, need regular, but "must" chiefly in the future and conditional feumaidh mi falbh "I must go"; am feum mi …? — Feumaidh.
faod may future and conditional faodaidh tu "you may"; nach fhaodadh duine … "that no one might …"
theab almost (did) past only theab mi tuiteam "I almost fell"
arsa, ars said past only, with direct speech ars esan
thalla, tiugainn, trobhad go!, come on!, come here! imperative only thalla dhachaigh!

Necessity and ability are more often expressed with the copula and prepositions (is fheudar dhomh, is urrainn dhomh, tha agam ri): Sentences §5.3–5.4.

7. The copula

The copula is links two noun phrases and fronts a stressed element; bi is used for location, state and existence (Sentences §1.2–1.4). The copula has two tense forms: a present (also used for the future) and a past that is also the conditional. It is unstressed and has no verbal noun or imperative. The older tongue kept past and conditional apart; Dia-thìris has one form, bu, for both.

7.1 Forms

present, future past, conditional
affirmative is, 's bu + L; b' before a vowel and fh + vowel
negative chan (before vowels, pronouns and most nouns), cha before a consonant in fixed phrases (cha toil leam) cha bu + L; cha b'
question an, am (before labials) am bu, am b'
negative question nach nach bu, nach b'
"that" gur, gur e gum bu, gum b'
"that … not" nach nach bu
"if" mas (mas e), ma 's nam bu, nam b'
"if not" mur, mura mura bu
relative (affirmative) as, 's a bu, a b'
relative (negative) nach nach bu
"because" a chionn 's gur a chionn 's gum bu

7.2 The copula with pronouns

When the predicate is a definite noun or a pronoun, the copula is followed by a third-person pronoun (e, i, iad) that anticipates it: Is i Aisling an ceannard "Aisling is the leader"; Is e seo an sceul "this is the tale"; Chan e mise a rinn e "it was not I who did it". With an emphatic personal pronoun the copula takes it directly: Is mise Eilidh, Is tusa an t-oide.

present past/conditional
affirmative is e, is i, is iad; is mise, is tusa b' e, b' i, b' iad; bu mhise, bu tusa
negative chan e, chan i, chan iad cha b' e, cha b' i, cha b' iad
question an e?, an i?, an iad? am b' e?, am b' i?
answers 'S e. / Chan e. B' e. / Cha b' e.

7.3 Fixed copula phrases

Many common predicates are an adjective or noun with the copula and a preposition. Their tense is carried by the copula alone:

present past/conditional meaning
is toil leam bu toil leam I like / would like
is fheàrr leam b' fheàrr leam I prefer / would prefer
is urrainn dhomh b' urrainn dhomh I can / could
is aithne dhomh b' aithne dhomh I know (a person, a place)
is fheudar dhomh b' fheudar dhomh I must / had to
is còir dhomh bu chòir dhomh I ought
is leamsa e bu leamsa e it is mine / was mine
is math sin bu mhath sin that is good / would be good
is dòcha bu dòcha perhaps / it was likely
is annsa leam b' annsa leam I love best

Bu toil leam keeps toil plain by long usage (bu thoil leam is also heard). The superlative of adjectives is a relative copula clause (as motha, a bu mhotha, §4.4). Clefts with is ann (is ann dhutsa a bha am bradan an dàn) and is e … a belong to Sentences §1.6.

8. Numerals

8.1 Cardinals: the decimal count

The numerals have a counting form, used alone (in counting, arithmetic, telling the time), and an attributive form, used before a noun. The counting form of 1–19 takes the particle a (a h- before a vowel).

counting with a noun mutation and number of the noun
0 neoni —
1 a h-aon aon L with dental block, singular: aon bhàta, aon chù, aon taigh
2 a dhà dà L, dual (§3.6): dà bhàta, dà làimh
3 a trì trì plural: trì coin, trì bàtaichean
4 a ceithir ceithir plural
5 a còig còig plural
6 a sia sia plural
7 a seachd seachd plural
8 a h-ochd ochd plural
9 a naoi naoi plural
10 a deich deich plural
11 a h-aon deug aon … deug aon bhàta deug, aon taigh deug
12 a dhà dheug dà … dheug dà bhàta dheug (dheug is lenited after the dual)
13–19 a trì deug … trì … deug trì bàtaichean deug (see below)
20 fichead fichead singular: fichead bàta
30 trithead trithead singular
40 ceathrad
50 caogad
60 seascad
70 seachdad
80 ochdad
90 naochad
100 ceud ceud singular: ceud bliadhna
1000 mìle mìle singular: mìle long
1,000,000 millean millean singular

Tens and units. Dia-thìris joins a ten and a unit without a conjunction: fichead aon 21, ceathrad còig 45, naochad naoi 99. No 's "and" stands between them, as it does in the count by twenties (§8.2); the two are simply set side by side. The noun follows the whole numeral in the singular: ceathrad còig bàta.

13–19. A noun between the unit and deug stands in the plural in careful speech and in writing, as it has been of old: trì bàtaichean deug, còig coin deug. The singular (trì bàta deug) is heard in everyday speech, and is the only form for the nouns that stay singular after every numeral, such as bliadhna, latha.

Hundreds and thousands. Ceud and mìle are nouns: dà cheud 200 (lenited after dà), trì ceud 300, ochd ceud 800; dà mhìle 2000, trì mìle. Compound numbers run from largest to smallest: mìle ochd ceud ceathrad ochd 1848. A noun after them is singular: trì ceud bliadhna.

8.2 The vigesimal count

The older count by twenties is understood everywhere and used for ages, in old texts and in tales (The grammar in brief §10). Twenty is the unit, and the units above it join with air + lenited fhichead ("on twenty"):

vigesimal with a noun
20 fichead fichead bliadhna
21 aon air fhichead aon bhliadhna air fhichead
25 còig air fhichead còig bliadhna fichead (noun inside)
30 deich air fhichead deich bliadhna fichead
40 dà fhichead dà fhichead bliadhna
50 dà fhichead 's a deich dà fhichead bliadhna 's a deich
60 trì fichead trì fichead bliadhna
80 ceithir fichead
100 ceud (older còig fichead)

Tha e trì fichead bliadhna 's a deich a dh'aois "he is seventy years old". Bliadhna, latha and uair stay singular after every numeral (§3.9).

8.3 Ordinals

ordinal mutation ordinal
1st a' chiad L with dental block: a' chiad bhliadhna, a' chiad turas 11th an t-aonamh … deug
2nd an dàrna (an dara) none 12th an dàrna … deug
3rd an treas (an tritheamh) none 20th am ficheadamh
4th an ceathramh none 30th an tritheadamh
5th an còigeamh none 100th an ceudamh
6th an siathamh none 1000th am mìleamh
7th an seachdamh none last mu dheireadh: an latha mu dheireadh
8th an t-ochdamh none
9th an naoidheamh none
10th an deicheamh none

Ordinals take the article and precede the noun, which is singular: an seachdamh leanabh "the seventh child" (tale of the water horse), an treas latha deug "the thirteenth day". The ordinal suffix is -amh/-eamh, and ordinals of the decimal tens take it too (an ceathradamh "fortieth").

8.4 Personal numerals

Persons are counted with the personal numerals, nouns that take a following genitive plural (lenited, strong where it exists) or de:

numeral example
2 dithis dithis bhalach "two boys"; dithis againn "two of us"
3 triùir triùir chloinne "three children"; triùir mhac "three sons"
4 ceathrar ceathrar bhràithrean
5 còignear
6 sianar sianar dhiubh "six of them" (tale of the water horse)
7 seachdnar seachdnar chloinne
8 ochdnar
9 naoinear
10 deichnear

They are used for people only, and above ten the cardinals take over. They take the genitive as collectives do, for at root each is a noun for a company of so many: triùir, a group of three.

8.5 Fractions, multiples, distributives

form example
half leth m. (+ L as a prefix) leth-uair "half an hour", leth an arain; dà uair gu leth "two and a half hours"
third trian m. dà thrian "two thirds"
quarter cairteal m.; ceathramh m. cairteal na h-uarach "a quarter of an hour"
fifth, tenth … the ordinal as a noun: còigeamh, deicheamh, or an còigeamh cuid an deicheamh cuid "the tenth part"
once, twice aon uair, dà uair, trì uairean
double dùbailte
one each fear an duine "one per man", tè an duine

8.6 Dates and time

Days (always with Di-, written solid, and outside caol le caol): Diluain, Dimàirt, Diciadain, Diardaoin, Dihaoine, Disathairne, Didòmhnaich. Months take the article:

month nom. "of ___" (de + article + dative) month nom. "of ___"
January am Faoilleach den Fhaoilleach July an t-Iuchar den Iuchar
February an Gearran den Ghearran August an Lùnastal den Lùnastal
March am Màrt den Mhàrt September an t-Sultain (f.) den t-Sultain
April an Giblean den Ghiblean October an Dàmhair (f.) den Dàmhair
May an Cèitean den Chèitean November an t-Samhain (f.) den t-Samhain
June an t-Ògmhios den Ògmhios December an Dùbhlachd (f.) den Dùbhlachd

A date is the ordinal + latha + de: an ceathramh latha den Ghiblean "the fourth of April"; Diluain, an treas latha deug den t-Samhain "Monday the thirteenth of November". A year: anns a' bhliadhna mìle ochd ceud ceathrad ochd "in the year 1848", as the old count of the Diosal wrote it. A year of one of the eras now in use takes the era after it in the genitive: anns a' bhliadhna fichead seachd de Linn an Dubhain "in the year 27 of the Dubhan Era", written DE 27. Genitives of the months appear in mìos na Samhna "the month of November", Latha Bealltainn "May Day".

Time of day uses uair "hour": aig uair "at one o'clock", aig dà uair, aig trì uairean, leth-uair an dèidh ceithir "half past four", cairteal gu còig "a quarter to five".

9. Derivational morphology

Dia-thìris builds words from its own stems with its own suffixes and prefixes, and by compounding. Every derived word obeys caol le caol inside itself, so suffixes come in broad and slender pairs chosen by the last vowel of the stem.

9.1 Agent nouns

All are masculine; a woman is named with ban- (§9.5) or with bean-.

suffix from examples
-air / -(e)ir nouns iascair "fisherman" (iasc), sealgair "hunter" (sealg), dorsair "doorkeeper" (doras), clàrsair "harper" (clàrsach)
-adair / -eadair verbs and nouns scrìobhadair "writer", creachadair "raider" (creach), sealbhadair "owner" (sealbh), dealbhadair "painter", lìonadair "filler"
-aiche / -iche verbs, esp. -ich verbs suathaiche "grazer" (suath), stiùiriche "steerer" (stiùir), rannsaiche "searcher" (rannsaich), cuiriche "sower" (cuir), bàthaiche "drowner" (bàth)
-aire / -eire verbs slugaire "swallower" (sluig), cladhaire "digger" (cladhaich), snìomhaire "twister" (snìomh)
-ach / -each places, qualities Dia-thìreach, Tuathach, coigreach "stranger"
periphrastic fear-, bean-, neach-, luchd- + genitive or participle fear-pòsta "husband", bean-phòsta "wife", neach-cuibhrinn "stakeholder", luchd-turais "travellers"

Fear- and neach- compounds pluralise as luchd- (luchd-turais) or by the head (fir-phòsta). The agent suffixes are the most productive in the kennings (§10): suathaiche-nèimh, slugaire-solais, bàthaiche-teine, cuiriche-òir, cladhaire-chnàmh.

9.2 Abstract nouns

suffix gender from examples
-as / -eas m. adjectives sonas "happiness" (sona), donas "evil" (dona), gliocas "wisdom" (glic), maitheas "goodness" (math), ceartas "justice" (ceart), càirdeas "friendship" (caraid)
-adas / -eadas m. adjectives dorchadas "darkness" (dorcha), bòidheachas "beauty"
-achd / -eachd f. nouns, adjectives, verbs rìoghachd "kingdom" (rìgh), bàrdachd "poetry" (bàrd), sceulachd "storytelling, tale" (sceul), fàisneachd "prophecy", coiseachd "walking", marcachd "riding"
-e f. adjectives (= the comparative form) gile "whiteness", òige "youth", doimhne "depth", àirde "height"
-(e)achas m. nouns iascachas "fishery", tuathanachas "farming"

9.3 Adjective-forming suffixes

suffix meaning examples
-ach / -each having, full of creagach "rocky" (creag), salach "dirty" (sal), feumach "needy" (feum), gaolach "loving" (gaol), craobhach "wooded"
-ail / -eil like, pertaining to fearail "manly", càirdeil "friendly", rìoghail "royal", làitheil "daily", bliadhnail "yearly", dùthchasail "native"
-mhor abounding in lìonmhor "numerous" (lìon "fill"), brìghmhor "full of substance", neartmhor "mighty", ceòlmhor "musical", cumhachdmhor "powerful"
-te / -ta participle (§6.7) briste, pòsta, loiscte, tollta
so- / do- prefix: easy / hard to (§9.5) so-dhèanta, do-dhèanta

-mhor is written the same after either class of vowel and stands outside caol le caol; it was once a word of its own, mòr "great", and keeps the freedom of one.

9.4 Diminutives

suffix gender examples
-an / -ean m. lochan "small loch", bothan "hut, cottage" (both), cnocan "hillock", sruthan "brook", leabhran "booklet", balachan "little boy"
-ag / -eag f. caileag "girl" (old caile), bileag "leaflet, ticket" (bile "leaf"), clachag "pebble", cuileag "fly", duilleag "leaf, page"

The diminutive takes its own gender regardless of the base: loch m. → lochan m., clach f. → clachag f., but bile m. → bileag f. Names take -an as an endearment and a patronymic suffix: Dubhan (dubh), Fionnan (fionn), Ciaran. The kennings use bileag for papers of every kind (bileag-turais "ticket", bileag-lùghdachaidh "coupon").

9.5 Prefixes

All the productive prefixes lenite what follows (with the usual exceptions, §1.2) and are hyphenated, except a few fused long ago (banacharaid "female friend", aineolach "ignorant", comhairle "counsel").

prefix meaning examples
mì- un-, mis-, bad mì-thoilichte "unhappy", mì-fhortan "misfortune", mì-chinnteach "uncertain", mì-rùn "ill will"
neo- not, un- neo-chiontach "innocent", neo-bhàsmhor "immortal", neo-ar-thaing "no thanks needed"; neoni "nothing, zero" (fused)
ath- re-, again, second ath-bhreith "rebirth", ath-shealladh "second sight, déjà vu", ath-ghleusadh "re-tuning", ath-bheothachadh "revival"
ban- female ban-rìgh "queen", ban-dia "goddess", ban-ghaisceach "heroine", ban-tighearna "lady" (dental block after n)
co-, comh- together, co- co-ogha "cousin", co-dhùnadh "decision", co-chomhairle "consultation", comh-fhreagairt "correspondence"
so- easy to, -able so-dhèanta "feasible", so-thuigsinn "easily understood", so-ruighinn "accessible"
do- hard to, un-…-able do-dhèanta "impossible", do-thuigsinn "incomprehensible"
fìor- true, genuine fìor-uisce "spring water", fìor-ghlan "pure"
ro- fore-, pre-; too ro-ràdh "preface", ro-shealladh "foresight", ro-mhath "very good"
fo- under, sub- fo-cheàrd "under-craftsman", fo-bhrìgh "hidden meaning", fo-thalamh "underground"
eadar- inter-, between eadar-theangachadh "translation", eadar-mheadhanach "intermediate"
dì- privative, de- dì-cheannadh "beheading", dì-mheas "contempt"
eu-, ea- negative eu-comasach "impossible", eu-dòchas "despair"
àrd-, prìomh-, sàr-, leth- chief, principal, excellent, half §4.5

9.6 Compounding

Dia-thìris has two kinds of compound, and both are old.

1. Close compounds (modifier first). An adjective, a preposed noun or a prefix comes first and lenites the head: àrd-rìgh "high king", prìomh-bhaile "chief town", mòr-shluagh "multitude", garbh-chrìochan "rough bounds", dubh-ghorm "dark blue", deagh-ghean "goodwill". The head (second element) gives the gender and takes the endings: na h-àrd-rìghrean, prìomh-bhailtean. The dental block applies loosely: free phrases keep it (seann taigh), fixed names may not (Seann-Dhaoine, §1.4).

2. Loose compounds (head first). A noun is followed by a genitive, a verbal noun in the genitive, or an adjective, and the pair is hyphenated once it names one thing: taigh-òsta "inn" (house of hosting), each-uisce "water-horse", bean-phòsta "wife", craiceann-ròin "seal-skin" (pl. craicnean-ròin), clach-chuimhne "memorial stone", taigh-freiceadain "watch-house". This is Dia-thìris's main word-building pattern and the pattern of every kenning (§10).

  • The head (first element) gives the gender and takes every inflection: an t-each-uisce, an eich-uisce (gen.), na h-eich-uisce; stad a' charbaid-iarainn "the stop of the train".
  • The describer is fixed in its genitive (or adjective) form, but it follows the lenition rules of §3.5, §3.8 and §4.1 for the head: after a feminine head an adjective is lenited (cèir-chruaidh) and a genitive often is (clach-chuimhne, fuil-ghuail); after any head an indefinite genitive plural is lenited (seanchas-dhaoine); after a slender plural head the describer lenites (eich-chuibhle).
  • Hyphens join the elements of a compound that names one thing; a free phrase is written apart (clach mhòr "a big stone", clach-mhòr would be a name). Caol le caol binds each hyphenated part separately, since it holds only inside one word.
  • Stress in a loose compound falls on both elements, the heavier on the describer (taigh-ÒSTA); in a close compound on the first (ÀRD-rìgh). See The sounds.

10. The kennings: how Dia-thìris names new things

10.1 How the kennings came about

Dia-thìr had no word for most of what the humans brought when they came, in the first years of the Anchor Era, and later the kingdom needed words for things of its own making. Dia-thìris took few of the humans' words for these things (The grammar in brief §13). For most of them its speakers made a name as the language had long named the each-uisce and the taigh-òsta: a loose compound of old roots that says what the thing does or what it is like. Such a name is called a kenning. The Dictionary lists 609 of them, each with its literal sense.

In its forms a kenning is an ordinary head-first loose compound (§9.6): a head noun, a describer in the genitive (or an adjective, a genitive plural, a prepositional phrase), hyphenated. It inflects through its head, pluralises through its head, and takes the head's gender. A small number of heads and describers recur, each carrying a fixed meaning, and this is what makes a new kenning easy to understand the first time it is heard.

10.2 How a new kenning is made

  1. Old roots. Speakers build from words long in the language, the words of the tales and of the bards (nèamh, speur, teine, gual, iarann, guth, dealbh, cuimhne, siubhal, suain, sceul), and from old borrowings for things known before about AE 20 (leabhar, cofaidh). Roots that came in with the humans' learning (tele-, fòn-, eileactr-, meatair) are not used.
  2. Head first, then the describer, hyphenated, the describer in the genitive where the grammar wants it.
  3. Two elements, three at most. Three-element kennings use a preposition or the article inside: teine-gun-lasair, gille-nan-soithichean.
  4. Each part obeys caol le caol.
  5. Mutation by the compound rules (§9.6): the describer is lenited after a feminine head when it is an adjective (and optionally when it is a genitive singular), and after any head when it is an indefinite genitive plural.

10.3 The patterns, with thirty-two examples

Genders and plurals are those of everyday use.

10.5 Inflecting a kenning

A kenning is a noun, and declines by its head (§3). Taking carbad-iarainn m. "train" and inntinn-iarainn f. "computer":

carbad-iarainn inntinn-iarainn
nom. sg. an carbad-iarainn an inntinn-iarainn
gen. sg. a' charbaid-iarainn (stad a' charbaid-iarainn "the train stop") na h-inntinne-iarainn
dat. sg. air a' charbad-iarainn air an inntinn-iarainn
nom. pl. na carbadan-iarainn na h-inntinnean-iarainn
gen. pl. nan carbadan-iarainn nan inntinnean-iarainn
with a possessive mo charbad-iarainn m' inntinn-iarainn
with an adjective carbad-iarainn mòr inntinn-iarainn mhòr

A kenning can itself become a head or a describer. Carbad gives stiùiriche-carbaid "driver" and bothan-carbaid "garage"; dealanach gives carbad-dealanaich and tobar-dealanaich "socket". So the kennings have become a living way of making words. The heads and describers of §10.4 are as good as suffixes with fixed meanings, and a speaker names a new thing by choosing a head for what it is and a describer for what it does.

Sentences

This chapter describes how Dia-thìris builds sentences: the clause and its two verbs "to be", aspect and the verbal noun, the particles, the passive and the impersonal, the experiencer constructions with prepositions, relative and subordinate clauses, the noun phrase, and the conventions of speech and writing. It closes with three sample texts with interlinear glosses: a dialogue, entries from the annals, and a proclamation.

The chapter cites a form and says how it is used. The full paradigms are in Word forms: the mutations (§1), the article (§2), noun cases and plurals (§3), adjectives and comparison (§4), pronouns and prepositional pronouns (§5), the verb with its impersonal and relative forms (§6), the copula (§7), and the numerals and dates (§8). Spelling, the mutations and a short account of word order are in The grammar in brief. Every example is numbered, written in Dia-thìris spelling, glossed word by word and translated (§0.2). Many are taken from the conversations and tales of the Texts chapter, and these are marked (T).

0. Conventions

0.1 Register: the Dia-thìris norm is the conservative one

Dia-thìris is the tongue of an old island that has long kept to itself, and its norm is the conservative one. For centuries the island's scribes and the library at Muileann chaol have held good speech close to the written language. Where the language has an older, literary construction beside a newer spoken one, the norm is the older, in speech as well as in writing (Word forms §0.1). The newer constructions are heard in casual talk, and this chapter marks them colloquial. Five things follow from this:

  1. Synthetic verb forms are preferred. The old present-future carries habitual and general statements (Òlaidh e uisce gach madainn), the conditional carries the past habitual (Sheasadh i aig an doras), and the synthetic first persons of the conditional and imperative are kept (sheasainn, sheasamaid, seasam, seasamaid). The periphrastic bidh e ag òl is correct but plainer.
  2. Case is used in full. Nouns take the genitive after a noun, after a verbal noun and after compound prepositions; adjectives agree with a genitive noun (taigh an duine mhòir); feminine nouns take their dative after simple prepositions (air a' chloich); the dual follows dà (dà làimh); the vocative is marked.
  3. The older relative and conditional forms are the norm. A prepositional relative puts its preposition before the relative particle (an taigh anns an robh mi, not an taigh a bha mi ann). The relative future in -(e)as is used after a, nuair a, ma and cho fad 's a. Conditional clauses keep the full sequence of tenses.
  4. Examples use old native vocabulary. When new things came to the island, it named most of them from its own old roots (The grammar in brief §13): a teacher is an oide, a doctor a lighiche, a telephone a guth-sreinge. The loans that came in with the humans at the Crossing and after, and are still heard (tidsear, dotair, oifis), are shunned in formal Dia-thìris.
  5. Old registers are represented. Proverbs, the formulas of the tale-teller, the quotative arsa, the jussive of proclamations and the terse verb-noun headings of the annals all appear in the examples, because a Dia-thìreach meets them daily.

Two kinds of note stand beside the rules. A note headed Older usage sets a construction beside its shape in the older language: the tongue of the bardic schools, whose verse the Library keeps, and the older speech behind it, known from the oldest leaves. Such notes explain, and add no rule. A note headed Usage marks a point where good Dia-thìris holds to a form that careless speech lets go.

0.2 Examples

Every example is numbered, written in Dia-thìris spelling (grave accents only; sc, never sg), glossed word by word, and translated. The glosses use the abbreviations of the Library's grammarians:

Gloss Meaning Gloss Meaning
1SG, 2PL, 3SG.M… person, number, gender COP copula (is, bu)
PRS present (tha, bheil) PST past
FUT present-future COND conditional
IMP imperative JUSS imperative of the 1st/3rd person ("let…")
REL relative particle or relative verb form REL.FUT relative future (-eas/-as, bhios)

VN verbal noun PROG progressive ag/a'

EMPH emphatic pronoun or suffix COMP, SUP comparative, superlative

at.1SG a prepositional pronoun (agam) in.3SG.M.POSS na = ann + a "in his"

Examples taken from the Texts chapter are marked (T).

1. The clause

1.1 Verb, subject, object

The Dia-thìris clause begins with the verb. The subject follows the verb, the object follows the subject, and everything else (prepositional phrases, adverbs of place, then adverbs of time) comes after that:

(1)   Chunnaic  an   t-iascair  an   ròn   air  a'   chladach   an-dè.
      see.PST   the  fisherman  the  seal  on   the  shore.DAT  yesterday
      ‘The fisherman saw the seal on the shore yesterday.’

(2)   Thug      am   bàrd  am   bradan  do  Fhionn.
      give.PST  the  poet  the  salmon  to  Fionn
      ‘The poet gave the salmon to Fionn. (T)’

The verb stands first in statements, questions and commands alike. A question or negative adds a particle before the verb and changes nothing else (§3):

(3)   Am  faca         an   t-iascair  an   ròn?
      Q   see.PST.DEP  the  fisherman  the  seal
      ‘Did the fisherman see the seal?’

(4)   Chan  fhaca        an   t-iascair  an   ròn.
      NEG   see.PST.DEP  the  fisherman  the  seal
      ‘The fisherman did not see the seal.’

Only three things can stand before the verb: a particle (negative, interrogative, conjunction, relative); the copula, which itself is a verb and brings its own fronted phrase with it (§1.6); and, in narrative, a scene-setting adverbial phrase, followed by a comma:

(5)   Aon  oidhche  ghealaich,  chaidh  e      sìos  chun  a'   chladaich.
      one  night    moon.GEN    go.PST  3SG.M  down  to    the  shore.GEN
      ‘One moonlit night, he went down to the shore. (T)’

A pronoun object tends to move to the end of its clause, after a short prepositional phrase, while a heavy noun object stays next to the verb or moves to the end in its place:

(6)   Dh'fhalaich  e      fo     a    chòta  e.
      hide.PST     3SG.M  under  his  coat   3SG.M
      ‘He hid it under his coat. (T)’

(7)   Chuir    i      uimpe        an   craiceann.
      put.PST  3SG.F  about.3SG.F  the  skin
      ‘She put on the skin. (T)’

The verb is followed by its subject even when the subject is long; Dia-thìris does not move a heavy subject forward. What English does with a heavy subject Dia-thìris does with a relative clause after the subject, or with a cleft (§1.6).

1.2 The two verbs "to be"

Dia-thìris has two verbs that English translates as "to be":

  • the substantive verb bi (tha, bha, bidh, bhiodh…), which says that something exists, is somewhere, or is in some state;
  • the copula is (is, bu), which links a subject to what it is: a class it belongs to, an identity, or a property treated as essential. The copula also fronts a phrase for emphasis.

The choice is never free. It depends on what kind of thing follows.

After "be" in English Dia-thìris Example
an adjective (a state) bi Tha an cala beag.
a place, a prepositional phrase bi Tha e air a' chladach.
a verbal noun with ag, air, ri, gu bi Tha i a' scrìobhadh.
existence ("there is") bi + ann Tha stoirm ann.
an indefinite noun (class) copula, or bi + ann + possessive Is iascair e. / Tha e na iascair.
a definite noun or name (identity) copula Is e Tormod an t-iascair.
emphasis on one part copula + fronted part Is ann an-dè a thàinig e.

1.3 The substantive verb

Bi takes an adjective, a prepositional phrase or an adverb as its predicate:

(8)   Tha     an   t-eilean  mòr.
      be.PRS  the  island    big
      ‘The island is big.’

(9)   Bha     a'   mhuir  ciùin  fad     na   h-oidhche.
      be.PST  the  sea    calm   length  the  night.GEN
      ‘The sea was calm all night.’

(10)  Bidh    na   longan  anns  a'   chala    a-màireach.
      be.FUT  the  ships   in    the  harbour  tomorrow
      ‘The ships will be in the harbour tomorrow.’

Existence is bi + subject + ann "in it", literally "X is in it":

(11)  Tha     stoirm  ann.
      be.PRS  storm   in.3SG.M
      ‘There is a storm.’

(12)  Bha     siud  ann       uair  iascair.
      be.PST  yon   in.3SG.M  once  fisherman
      ‘There was once a fisherman. (tale opening, T)’

(13)  Chan  eil         duilgheadas  ann.
      NEG   be.PRS.DEP  difficulty   in.3SG.M
      ‘There is no difficulty. (No problem.)’

Weather is expressed as existence or as a state of the day, with the feminine pronoun i for the weather itself: Tha an t-uisce ann "it's raining" (the rain is in it), Tha i fuar an-diugh "it's cold today".

A non-verbal predicate with bi + ann + possessive classifies the subject: literally "he is in his fisherman". The possessive agrees with the subject, and ann + possessive fuses into nam, nad, na, na, nar, nur, nan (see the table in §2.7):

(14)  Tha     e      na             iascair.
      be.PRS  3SG.M  in.3SG.M.POSS  fisherman
      ‘He is a fisherman.’

(15)  Bha     i      na             bean-phòsta  chòir.
      be.PST  3SG.F  in.3SG.F.POSS  wife         kind
      ‘She was a kind wife. (T)’

(16)  Nuair  a    bha     mi   nam          bhalach,  bha     mi   a'    fuireach  aig
      when   REL  be.PST  1SG  in.1SG.POSS  boy       be.PST  1SG  PROG  live.VN   at
      Ceann  Dubh.
      Ceann  Dubh
      ‘When I was a boy, I lived at Ceann Dubh.’

This construction suits a role or a stage of life, something one is at the moment or became (Tha e na bhodach a-nis "he's an old man now"). The copula (§1.4) states what a thing is.

1.4 The copula: classification and identification

The present copula is is ('s unstressed, and written 'S at the start of a sentence in speech and dialogue). Its past and conditional form is bu (b' before a vowel or fh), which lenites. Negative chan, cha bu / cha b'; interrogative an, am bu; negative interrogative nach, nach bu. The copula has no future of its own; the present covers it. The full table is in The grammar in brief §7.4 and Word forms §7.

Classification ("X is a Y", Y indefinite). The oldest and most literary pattern is copula + predicate noun + subject. It is the Dia-thìris norm in formal prose, proverbs and verse:

(17)  Is   iascair    e.
      COP  fisherman  3SG.M
      ‘He is a fisherman.’

(18)  Is   Dia-thìreach  mi,  agus  is   Tuathach    i.
      COP  Dia-thìreach  1SG  and   COP  northerner  3SG.F
      ‘I am a Dia-thìreach, and she is a Tuathach.’

(19)  Bu       ghobha  a    athair.
      COP.PST  smith   his  father
      ‘His father was a smith.’

The everyday pattern puts a pronoun after the copula and turns the rest into a relative clause: "it is a fisherman that is in him":

(20)  Is   e      iascair    a    th'     ann.
      COP  3SG.M  fisherman  REL  be.PRS  in.3SG.M
      ‘He is a fisherman.’

(21)  'S   e      oileanach  a    th'     annam.
      COP  3SG.M  student    REL  be.PRS  in.1SG
      ‘I am a student.’

(22)  Is   e      seòladair  a    th'     ann.
      COP  3SG.M  sailor     REL  be.PRS  in.3SG.M
      ‘He's a sailor. (T)’

(23)  Chan     e      bàrd  a    bh'     innte,    ach  scrìobhaiche.
      NEG.COP  3SG.M  poet  REL  be.PST  in.3SG.F  but  scribe
      ‘She was not a poet but a scribe.’

The a th' ann pattern is obligatory when the predicate noun has an adjective or a long modifier (Is e seòladair math a th' ann), and in questions with dè: Dè a th' ann? "What is it?"

Identification ("X is the Y", both definite). The copula is followed by a pronoun that stands for the subject, then the subject, then the predicate:

(24)  Is   e      Tormod  an   t-iascair.
      COP  3SG.M  Tormod  the  fisherman
      ‘Tormod is the fisherman.’

(25)  Is   i      Eilidh  a'   bhana-bhàrd.
      COP  3SG.F  Eilidh  the  poetess
      ‘Eilidh is the poetess.’

(26)  Is   iad  na   Dia-thìrich  sluagh  an   eilein.
      COP  3PL  the  Dia-thìrich  people  the  island.GEN
      ‘The Dia-thìrich are the people of the island.’

(27)  B'       e      Fionn  an   t-ainm  a    bh'     air.
      COP.PST  3SG.M  Fionn  the  name    REL  be.PST  on.3SG.M
      ‘Fionn was his name. (T)’

Usage. The pronoun after the copula agrees with the subject: e for a man or a masculine noun, i for a woman or a feminine noun, iad for a plural. Careless speech often lets 's e stand for all three; good writing never does.

With a demonstrative or a personal pronoun as subject, the pronoun follows the copula directly; the emphatic pronouns mise, thusa… are used, and no e is added:

(28)  Is   mise      Eilidh.
      COP  1SG.EMPH  Eilidh
      ‘I am Eilidh. (T)’

(29)  Is   e      seo   an   cala.
      COP  3SG.M  this  the  harbour
      ‘This is the harbour.’

(30)  An     e      seo   a'   chiad  turas    agaibh  an-seo?
      Q.COP  3SG.M  this  the  first  journey  at.2PL  here
      ‘Is this your first time here? (T)’

Copula + adjective. The copula with an adjective predicate states a lasting quality, a judgement, or a general truth. It is common in proverbs and formal speech, and in fixed expressions of opinion:

(31)  Is   mòr  an   t-eilean  seo.
      COP  big  the  island    this
      ‘Great is this island.’

(32)  Is   domhainn  na   h-uisceachan  ciùin.
      COP  deep      the  waters        calm
      ‘Still waters run deep.’

(33)  Is   fìor  sin.
      COP  true  that
      ‘That is true.’

(34)  Bu        mhath  sin.
      COP.COND  good   that
      ‘That would be good.’

Tha an t-eilean mòr reports the island's size; Is mòr an t-eilean exclaims or asserts it. Many fixed predicates are copula + adjective or noun + preposition: is toil le, is fheàrr le, is urrainn do, is aithne do, is èiginn do, is fhiach (§5).

Older usage. In the oldest verse the copula is already is, with the negative nì and the past ba; bu is the old past and conditional budh. The "X is in his Y" construction (tha e na iascair) is younger. It first appears in the middle period of the language, and it spread as the copula's classifying use grew formal.

1.5 Answers with the copula

The copula is answered with the copula and its first element: An e seo an cala? — 'S e. / Chan e. "Is this the harbour? — It is. / It isn't." An toil leat scadan? — 'S toil. / Cha toil. See §3.5.

1.6 Fronting and clefts: is e and is ann

Any part of a clause except the verb can be put in focus by fronting it with the copula and turning the rest of the clause into a relative clause. Which pronoun the copula takes depends on what is fronted:

  • a noun, a noun phrase or a pronoun is fronted with is e (is i, is iad by agreement for a definite noun; plain is before an emphatic pronoun);
  • anything else (a prepositional phrase, an adverb, an adjective, a verbal-noun phrase) is fronted with is ann.
(35)  Chunnaic  Calum  an   long  an-dè.
      see.PST   Calum  the  ship  yesterday
      ‘Calum saw the ship yesterday. (neutral)’

(36)  Is   e      Calum  a    chunnaic  an   long  an-dè.
      COP  3SG.M  Calum  REL  see.PST   the  ship  yesterday
      ‘It was Calum who saw the ship yesterday.’

(37)  Is   i      an   long  a    chunnaic  Calum  an-dè.
      COP  3SG.F  the  ship  REL  see.PST   Calum  yesterday
      ‘It was the ship that Calum saw yesterday.’

(38)  Is   ann       an-dè      a    chunnaic  Calum  an   long.
      COP  in.3SG.M  yesterday  REL  see.PST   Calum  the  ship
      ‘It was yesterday that Calum saw the ship.’

(39)  Is   mise      a    rinn    e.
      COP  1SG.EMPH  REL  do.PST  3SG.M
      ‘It was I who did it.’

(40)  Is   ann       à     Dhia-thìr  a    tha     mi.
      COP  in.3SG.M  from  Dia-thìr  REL  be.PRS  1SG
      ‘I am from Dia-thìr.’

(41)  Is   ann       scìth  a    tha     mi,  chan     ann       tinn.
      COP  in.3SG.M  tired  REL  be.PRS  1SG  NEG.COP  in.3SG.M  ill
      ‘I'm tired, not ill.’

(42)  Is   ann       a'    tilleadh   a    bha     iad.
      COP  in.3SG.M  PROG  return.VN  REL  be.PST  3PL
      ‘They were coming back (not going).’

The copula keeps present form in a present or neutral frame, even for past events (Is e Calum a chunnaic); in a narrative in the past it may itself go into the past: B' e Calum a chunnaic an long. Negative chan e / chan ann, question an e / an ann, negative question nach e / nach ann:

(43)  An     ann       dhutsa       a    bha     am   bradan  an  dàn?
      Q.COP  in.3SG.M  to.2SG.EMPH  REL  be.PST  the  salmon  in  fate
      ‘Was it for you that the salmon was destined?’

(44)  Cha  b'       e      ainm  a    thagh       iad  fhèin  a    bh'     ann.
      NEG  COP.PST  3SG.M  name  REL  choose.PST  3PL  self   REL  be.PST  in.3SG.M
      ‘It was not a name they chose themselves. (T)’

A fronted adjective with is ann is common in exclamation and contrast; the older pattern puts the adjective directly after the copula (Is fuar an oidhche!). A cleft with is ann + mar sin ends many tales: Agus is ann mar sin a tha iad chun an latha an-diugh "and that is how they are to this day" (T).

Older usage. Clefting with the copula is old; the oldest verse already fronts with is è and with the copula + a prepositional phrase. The ann of is ann is the prepositional pronoun "in it", used as a dummy predicate.

2. Aspect and the verbal noun

Dia-thìris tense is carried by the inflected verb; aspect is carried by bi + a preposition + the verbal noun (VN). The verbal noun is a noun: it takes the article, governs a genitive, and takes a possessive for a pronoun object. The preposition says where the subject stands in relation to the action: ag "at" it (in progress), air "on, after" it (done), ri "at, engaged in" it, gu "towards" it (about to happen).

2.1 The progressive: ag / a'

Ag before a vowel, a' before a consonant. The progressive describes an action in progress. It is also the ordinary present of all verbs except bi, since the old simple present survives only in the present-future (§2.9):

(45)  Tha     mi   a'    leughadh.
      be.PRS  1SG  PROG  read.VN
      ‘I am reading.’

(46)  Tha     i      ag    òl        uisce.
      be.PRS  3SG.F  PROG  drink.VN  water.GEN
      ‘She is drinking water.’

(47)  Bha     na   mnathan  a'    dannsadh  air  a'   ghainmhich.
      be.PST  the  women    PROG  dance.VN  on   the  sand.DAT
      ‘The women were dancing on the sand.’

(48)  Bidh    sinn  a'    feitheamh  riut.
      be.FUT  1PL   PROG  wait.VN    for.2SG
      ‘We will be waiting for you.’

A few verbs of perception and state take the progressive where English uses a simple tense: Tha mi a' tuigsinn "I understand", Tha mi a' smaoineachadh gu bheil "I think so", Tha e a' fuireach aig Ceann Dubh "he lives at Ceann Dubh". Verbs of position do not (they use the state construction, §2.7).

2.2 The perfect: air

Bi + air + VN is a perfect: the action is complete and its result holds. With tha it is a present perfect, with bha a pluperfect, with bidh a future perfect, with bhiodh a conditional perfect:

(49)  Tha     mi   air  tighinn  à     Cathair  dhearg.
      be.PRS  1SG  PRF  come.VN  from  Cathair  dhearg
      ‘I have come from Cathair dhearg. (T)’

(50)  Tha     sinn  air  ithe.
      be.PRS  1PL   PRF  eat.VN
      ‘We have eaten.’

(51)  Bha     i      air  tilleadh   mus     do   dhùisc    e.
      be.PST  3SG.F  PRF  return.VN  before  PST  wake.PST  3SG.M
      ‘She had returned before he woke.’

(52)  Bidh    sinn  air  ruigsinn  ron         oidhche.
      be.FUT  1PL   PRF  reach.VN  before.the  night
      ‘We will have arrived before night.’

(53)  Bhiodh   iad  air  falbh.
      be.COND  3PL  PRF  go.VN
      ‘They would have gone.’

Because air falbh also means "away", Tha e air falbh is both "he has gone" and "he is away"; the two senses are one.

An dèidh "after" is used like air, for an action just completed:

(54)  Tha     e      an dèidh  tighinn  a-steach.
      be.PRS  3SG.M  after     come.VN  in
      ‘He has just come in.’

2.3 The prospective: gu, a' dol a, an impis

Gu + VN (often gu bhith) is "about to", "due to":

(55)  Tha     mi   gu       bhith  deiseil.
      be.PRS  1SG  towards  be.VN  ready
      ‘I'm about to be ready.’

(56)  Bha     an   long  gu       falbh  nuair  a    thàinig   an   stoirm.
      be.PST  the  ship  towards  go.VN  when   REL  come.PST  the  storm
      ‘The ship was about to leave when the storm came.’

A' dol a + lenited VN is "going to", an intended or expected future:
